title: Baidu Profit Drops 68% as Revenue Declines for Fifth Straight Quarter
excerpt: China's search giant missed analyst estimates as intensifying AI competition from Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek erodes its core advertising business, while Fitch downgrades its credit rating.
body:
• Baidu's Q2 2026 net profit fell 68% to 2.32 billion yuan ($344.2 million), well below analyst estimates of 2.82 billion yuan, as its core search advertising business continues to shrink.
  • Revenue dropped 4.2% year-over-year to 31.325 billion yuan, marking the fifth consecutive quarterly decline as advertisers shift budgets to competing platforms.
  • Fitch Ratings downgraded Baidu to A- from A, citing weakening competitive position and cash flow pressures from heavy AI investment.
  • Baidu's Hong Kong-listed shares have fallen more than 20% year-to-date, underperforming the broader Hang Seng Tech Index.

A Deepening Revenue Slide

Baidu reported second-quarter revenue of 31.325 billion yuan ($4.65 billion), down 4.2% from the same period last year — its fifth straight quarterly decline. Net profit collapsed 68% to 2.32 billion yuan, missing the 2.82 billion yuan consensus estimate compiled by analysts polled by Reuters.

https://x.com/Techmeme/status/2089651189529170165

The results underscore a structural challenge for Baidu: its core online marketing services business, which still accounts for the majority of revenue, is losing ground to rivals who have integrated AI more aggressively into their consumer platforms. Alibaba's Tongyi Qianwen, ByteDance's Doubao and a wave of startups including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI have all launched competing AI products that are drawing users and advertisers away from Baidu's search ecosystem.

"Baidu's revenue decline reflects not just cyclical advertising weakness but a structural shift in how Chinese consumers discover information and make purchases."

— Wall Street Journal analysis

AI Investment Has Yet to Pay Off

CEO Robin Li has staked Baidu's future on artificial intelligence, positioning the company's Ernie Bot large language model as a core product and pledging to return it to the frontier of AI development. In the earnings call, Li said AI-powered services now account for roughly half of Baidu's general business revenue — but the metric obscures the fact that much of this revenue comes from existing search and cloud products that have been rebranded with AI features rather than genuinely new revenue streams.

Baidu's AI Cloud segment has shown growth, but not at the pace needed to offset the erosion in search advertising. The company faces a credibility gap: investors who bought the AI thesis when Ernie Bot launched in 2023 have watched the stock decline more than 20% year-to-date on the Hong Kong exchange, significantly underperforming the Hang Seng Tech Index.

Fitch Downgrade Adds Pressure

Fitch Ratings lowered Baidu's credit rating to A- from A in early August, citing the company's weakening competitive position and the cash flow pressure created by sustained AI infrastructure spending. The downgrade raises Baidu's borrowing costs at a time when it is investing heavily in large language models, autonomous driving through its Apollo Go robotaxi unit and custom AI chip development.

Baidu's semiconductor subsidiary Kunlunxin, which designs AI accelerator chips, is expected to pursue an initial public offering in Hong Kong later this year. A successful listing could provide a capital infusion and a partial valuation unlock, but market conditions for Chinese tech IPOs remain challenging amid geopolitical tensions and weak investor sentiment.

"We will return Ernie to the frontier of AI. The competitive landscape is fierce, but Baidu has the engineering depth and data assets to compete."

— Robin Li, CEO, Baidu

Competitive Landscape Intensifies

The Chinese AI market has become one of the most crowded in the world. Alibaba open-sourced its most powerful model, Qwen 2.5, last week. ByteDance has embedded AI across TikTok's sister app Douyin. DeepSeek, a startup backed by quantitative trading firm High-Flyer, released models that rival much larger systems at a fraction of the training cost. Moonshot AI's Kimi chatbot has gained rapid consumer adoption.

For Baidu, the challenge is competing on two fronts simultaneously: defending its search advertising moat against platforms that are becoming AI-first, while investing enough in next-generation models to remain relevant. The Q2 results suggest it is losing ground on both.

What Investors Are Watching

Three catalysts could shift Baidu's trajectory in the second half of 2026. The Kunlunxin IPO, if executed at a strong valuation, would demonstrate that Baidu's chip capabilities have standalone value. Apollo Go's expansion into more Chinese cities could accelerate the robotaxi business toward profitability. And Ernie Bot's next major model update, expected before year-end, will test whether Baidu can narrow the gap with leading Chinese and American models.

For now, the market is skeptical. Baidu trades at a significant discount to its Chinese tech peers, and the fifth consecutive revenue decline suggests that management's AI pivot — however strategically sound — has not yet translated into growth that investors can price in.
